A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FLYT study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching renamed methods and reorganized appendix material.

before.justification: v1 reports original DataComp medium- and small-scale CLIP pretraining results, baseline reproductions, and ablations of scoring, mixing, downstream data, and sampling.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports additional accuracy-weighted aggregation comparisons and SCS batch-size sensitivity results.

M1.justification: v2 explicitly separates the feature extractor from the scorer and renames v1’s embedding-based FLYT as E-FLYT. These correspond to the existing frozen CLIP base and trainable head. The gradient updates, weighted CLIP loss, 12-input linear mixing, and SCS procedure are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use DataComp medium and small scales, the same 38 evaluation tasks, ImageNet downstream training, and the same 22-dataset downstream-data experiment. The DFN reproduction and classifier training datasets also remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds ImageNet-weighted standardized-sum baselines with weight ratios 2, 4, 8, and 16. Table 1 drops the standalone FLYT comparison row, although E-FLYT results remain elsewhere. NegCLIPLoss is renamed s-CLIPLoss; EcoDatum already appeared in v1’s Table 3.

E3.justification: v2 adds medium-scale SCS evaluations at sampling batch sizes G = 10K and 1M, alongside the existing 100K setting, holding alpha = 0.15 fixed (Table 13). Existing benchmark procedures, training budgets, model configurations, and downstream-data settings are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C.10 adds a focused test of sensitivity to SCS sampling batch size. Its repetition-penalty table largely redisplays the sweep already plotted in v1’s Figure 3. Existing initialization, loss, learning-rate, downstream-data, and input-removal ablations remain under reorganized appendix sections.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. Score standardization concerns model inputs rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: For SCS alpha = 0.15, Table 1 revises VTAB from 0.391 to 0.396 and average accuracy from 0.375 to 0.377; ImageNet remains 0.401. Table 2 changes Sum ImageNet/average scores from 0.324/0.339 to 0.327/0.331 and Standardized Sum from 0.344/0.361 to 0.348/0.360. Weighted-sum and batch-size results are added. Standalone FLYT and alpha = 0.25 retain ImageNet/average results elsewhere, but their distribution-shift, VTAB, and retrieval entries disappear. These are reporting changes, without evidence establishing a methodological performance gain.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.5 mathematically defines accuracy-based aggregation weights and their prescribed maximum-to-minimum ratio. The core loss definitions, downstream-loss formulas, and Appendix A gradient derivation remain unchanged apart from feature-vector notation.

C1.justification: The 40.1% ImageNet headline remains, while its stated advantage changes from 1.9 to 2.0 percentage points. v2 adds 37.7% average accuracy to the abstract and claims superiority over accuracy-weighted aggregation. The introduction changes its average-accuracy comparison from 1.3 points below the leaderboard best to 0.1 points below the best reproduced baseline, changing the comparison reference.

C2.justification: New Section 3.4 explains ImageNet training data as a downstream proxy and the broader evaluation average as evidence about unfamiliar tasks. Section 5 more explicitly acknowledges reliance on existing filters and qualifies proposed optimization remedies as requiring validation. The SCS discussion also describes the diversity–accuracy tradeoff as less apparent than v1 suggested.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 newly discloses FLOP estimates, 40/45 A100 hours for M-FLYT/E-FLYT, and approximately 100 minutes of single-CPU SCS sampling. Appendix C.5 documents the new baseline construction. The paper’s code, model, and data release links remain, but explicit HYPE and NegCLIPLoss repository links are removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against concurrent EcoDatum and metagradient-descent work, distinguishing their aggregation and per-example weighting from FLYT’s learned scorer. It adds MGD and Snorkel references and supplies a paper citation for the existing EcoDatum comparator.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative around FLYT as a framework with M-FLYT and E-FLYT implementations. It rewrites the introduction, reorganizes the method section, moves and consolidates v1’s standalone FLYT results into Appendix C.7, and extensively reorders Appendix C. This exceeds terminology and numbering edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains an explicit feature-extractor node; Algorithms 1–2 become side-by-side; Figure 2 and Table 2 are rearranged; and a new SCS Table 13 is added. Summary tables are shortened, and Figure 3’s caption correctly identifies left/right panels. Most other figures and table formats are retained.

improvement.justification: The accuracy-weighted baselines strengthen the evidence for learned mixing, while the SCS batch-size ablation and computational-cost disclosures improve validation and transparency. Clearer organization and qualified limitations also help. These gains outweigh the limited loss of category-level results and two baseline-code links; the core method and most empirical evidence remain unchanged.
